articles.title: My Story: Life, Work, and Creativity
articles.description: A personal story about my roots in Maybrat, my journey through life and work, and the digital projects I am building for the future.
articles.dek: A journey from Maybrat, Papua, shaped by life experiences, creativity, technology, and dreams for the future.
articles.intro: Every person has a story shaped by where they come from, the experiences they have lived through, and the dreams they continue to pursue. My story begins in Maybrat, Papua, and continues through my journey of learning, working, creating, and exploring the digital world.

sections.heading: My Roots in Maybrat
paragraphs: I come from Maybrat, Papua, a place with a rich natural environment and a strong cultural identity. Growing up with the beauty and character of Papua has been an important part of who I am and how I see the world.

One of the places that represents the beauty of my homeland is Lake Ayamaru. Its natural scenery is part of the landscape that makes the Maybrat region special. The place where we come from can become an important part of our identity, memories, and personal story.
My roots continue to remind me of where my journey began. Wherever life takes me, Maybrat and Papua will always be an important part of my story.

sections.heading: My Work and Passion
paragraphs: Throughout my journey, I have learned that hard work, patience, and the willingness to keep learning are important in building a better future.

Besides my work and daily responsibilities, I have developed a strong interest in the digital world. Technology has opened new opportunities for creativity, learning, communication, and sharing ideas with people beyond my local environment.

I enjoy exploring new technologies and learning how different digital tools can be used to create something meaningful. This interest has encouraged me to continue developing my skills and experimenting with new ideas.

sections.heading: What I Do and What I Am Building
paragraphs: Today, I spend much of my time learning and working in the digital world. I create and manage online content, build websites, experiment with artificial intelligence tools, and explore different ways to share stories and ideas with people around the world.

I work on projects involving digital publishing, social media content, AI-generated images and videos, website development, and online platforms. Through these projects, I continue learning how technology can be used to create useful, interesting, and engaging content.

I am also building my own digital projects step by step. Some of them focus on stories, technology, creativity, and online publishing. The process is not always easy, but every project gives me an opportunity to learn something new and improve my skills.

My goal is not simply to create content. I want to build something that can continue growing over time. By combining creativity, technology, and consistent learning, I hope to create digital projects that can reach people from different parts of the world.

images.caption: The beauty of Maybrat and Lake Ayamaru is an important part of my roots and personal story.

images.caption: Learning new technology has become an important part of my personal and creative journey.

images.alt: A digital workspace representing my creative projects and online work
images.caption: Creating digital content and building online projects are important parts of my journey.

articles.closing:
My story is still being written.

I come from Maybrat, Papua, and the experiences of my life continue to shape the person I am becoming. From the beauty of Ayamaru to the growing world of digital technology, my journey has taught me to keep learning, creating, and moving forward.

I do not know exactly where this journey will take me, but I believe every small step matters. I will continue building, learning, and creating with the hope that the things I make can reach people and inspire them in their own journeys.

The future is still ahead, and there is always something new to learn, something new to create, and another step to take.

articles.title: Lady Gaga Welcomes Her First Baby With Fiancé Michael Polansky
articles.description: Lady Gaga and fiancé Michael Polansky have welcomed their first child together, marking a meaningful personal milestone for the superstar.
articles.dek: The superstar and her partner quietly begin parenthood after years of sharing her hopes of starting a family.
articles.intro: Lady Gaga has welcomed her first child with fiancé Michael Polansky, ushering in a major new personal chapter for the global icon. The happy news marks the fulfillment of an ambition the singer and actress has openly shared for years.

sections.heading: A Longtime Dream Realized
paragraphs: Reports from outlets including PEOPLE and Vogue confirmed the arrival of the couple's first baby, noting that details such as the child's name and sex have remained private.

Motherhood is a milestone Gaga has reflected on repeatedly across her career. In a 2024 Vogue interview, she spoke openly about love, family, and her connection with Polansky, acknowledging that having children was a long-held personal aspiration.

sections.heading: A Bond Built Away from the Spotlight
paragraphs: Gaga and Polansky began dating around 2019 and became publicly known as a couple in 2020. Their bond deepened significantly during the COVID-19 pandemic, when they spent an extended period together in Malibu away from the demands of public life.

Polansky has maintained a relatively private profile compared to Gaga's world-famous persona. Following their engagement in 2024, the couple continued to safeguard their private life, keeping their focus grounded as they prepared to expand their family.

sections.heading: A Quiet Family Milestone
paragraphs: Known affectionately by millions of fans worldwide as Mother Monster, Gaga now experiences motherhood in the most literal and personal sense. While supporters celebrated the arrival, the family has maintained their privacy, with Gaga's representatives withholding immediate public comment.

After years defined by high-profile tours, Grammy Awards, and Hollywood screen roles, this next chapter gives Gaga and Polansky the chance to savor family life away from the red carpets and camera flashes.

articles.title: The Real Story Behind Santa Claus: 4 Facts About Saint Nicholas
articles.description: Discover the real story behind Santa Claus and learn how Saint Nicholas, a generous Christian bishop, inspired one of the world's most beloved Christmas traditions.
articles.dek: The beloved Christmas figure of Santa Claus has a fascinating connection to Saint Nicholas, a fourth-century Christian bishop remembered for his extraordinary generosity and kindness.
articles.intro: Every Christmas, millions of children around the world eagerly wait for Santa Claus, the cheerful old man with a white beard, a red suit, and a sack full of presents. But behind this beloved Christmas character lies a fascinating historical story. Santa Claus was inspired in part by a real Christian figure known as Saint Nicholas, a bishop remembered for his generosity, compassion, and kindness toward people in need. His legacy dates back more than 1,600 years and continues to influence Christmas traditions around the world.

sections.heading: Saint Nicholas Was a Real Christian Bishop
paragraphs: Long before Santa Claus became a popular Christmas character, Saint Nicholas was remembered as a Christian bishop who lived during the fourth century.

He served as the Bishop of Myra, a city located in what is now modern-day Turkey. Although historical information about his personal life is limited, Christian traditions have preserved stories about his faith and generosity.

Nicholas became especially respected for helping vulnerable people, particularly children and poor families. His reputation gradually spread throughout Europe, where many communities honored him as an example of Christian kindness.

sections.heading: The Famous Story of Secretly Giving Gold to Three Poor Girls
paragraphs: One of the most famous legends associated with Saint Nicholas involves a poor father and his three daughters.
According to the traditional story, the family was experiencing extreme financial difficulties. The father could not afford the dowries needed for his daughters to marry.

When Nicholas learned about their situation, he decided to help without seeking recognition. According to the legend, he secretly delivered bags of gold to the family, providing the financial assistance they desperately needed.
This act of generosity became one of the most important stories associated with Saint Nicholas and helped establish his connection with the tradition of secretly giving gifts.

sections.heading: How Saint Nicholas Became Santa Claus
paragraphs: The transformation of Saint Nicholas into Santa Claus happened gradually over many centuries.
In the Netherlands, Saint Nicholas became known as Sinterklaas. He was traditionally portrayed as a white-bearded religious figure who brought gifts to children around December 6.
Dutch settlers later brought these traditions to North America. Over time, the name Sinterklaas evolved into Santa Claus.

During the nineteenth century, American writers and illustrators helped shape the modern character. Clement Clarke Moore's famous 1823 poem, A Visit from St. Nicholas, popularized the image of a magical gift-giver arriving in a sleigh pulled by reindeer.
Illustrator Thomas Nast also contributed to the familiar appearance of Santa Claus, including his round figure and association with the North Pole.

sections.heading: The Meaning of Santa Claus Goes Beyond Christmas Presents
paragraphs: Although modern Santa Claus is often associated with presents, shopping, and Christmas celebrations, the story of Saint Nicholas carries a deeper message.
His traditional legacy reminds people that generosity does not always need public recognition. Helping someone in need can be meaningful even when nobody knows who performed the good deed.
The story also reflects values that remain important during the Christmas season: compassion, kindness, humility, and concern for people experiencing hardship.
For Christians, Saint Nicholas offers an example of putting faith into action by caring for others.
Perhaps the most meaningful lesson behind Santa Claus is not the presents delivered on Christmas Eve, but the spirit of giving that inspired the tradition in the first place.

bibleVerse.text: “Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord, and he will reward them for what they have done.”

articles.closing:
The story of Santa Claus is more than a Christmas legend. Behind the familiar red suit and cheerful smile is the inspiring legacy of Saint Nicholas, a Christian bishop whose generosity became a symbol of kindness and compassion.

His story reminds us that the true meaning of giving is not measured by the value of a present, but by the love and care behind it. As Christmas brings families and communities together, the example of Saint Nicholas encourages everyone to share kindness, help those in need, and spread joy without expecting anything in return.

Perhaps that is the greatest lesson Santa Claus continues to teach the world: the spirit of Christmas lives not only in the gifts we receive, but also in the goodness we give to others.

articles.title: The First Baby: What Every Mother Goes Through During Childbirth
articles.description: A fact-based guide to first childbirth, the mother's body, newborn adaptation, early breastfeeding, and recovery after delivery.
articles.dek: A baby's first cry marks a new beginning, but childbirth also involves a remarkable physical process and a period of recovery for the mother.
articles.intro: The birth of a first child is a major moment for a family. For a mother, it involves more than meeting her newborn: her body goes through labour and delivery, then begins recovering while the baby adapts to life outside the womb. Medical guidance from the NHS and the World Health Organization helps explain what happens during these first hours and days. Every birth is different, so these facts describe common processes rather than a promise of what every mother will experience.

sections.heading: 1. The First Labour Can Take Time
paragraphs: During labour, the cervix gradually softens, thins, and opens so the baby can pass through the birth canal. In a first pregnancy, the process may take many hours. The length varies from one person to another and can depend on several medical and personal factors.

The NHS describes labour in stages, from the beginning of cervical changes to the birth of the baby and the delivery of the placenta. A first birth does not follow an identical timetable for every mother.

sections.heading: 2. Contractions Help the Baby Move Down
paragraphs: Contractions happen when the muscles of the uterus tighten and relax. As labour progresses, contractions generally become stronger, longer, and closer together. They help the cervix open and move the baby down through the birth canal.
Pain and pressure can be felt in the abdomen, back, or pelvis. The experience differs widely, and a maternity team can explain pain-relief and support options during labour.

sections.heading: 3. Labour Continues After the Baby Is Born
paragraphs: The birth of the baby is not always the final stage of labour. The placenta, sometimes called the afterbirth, must also be delivered. The uterus continues contracting to help the placenta separate and to reduce bleeding.
Midwives and doctors monitor the mother after delivery, including her bleeding and general condition. This is an important part of safe childbirth care.

sections.heading: 4. Skin-to-Skin Contact Can Support Bonding
paragraphs: When the mother and baby are clinically well, placing the newborn directly against the mother's bare chest can help keep the baby warm and support early bonding. It can also help breastfeeding get started.
Sometimes medical care means immediate skin-to-skin contact must be delayed. If that happens, bonding and breastfeeding can still be supported when mother and baby are ready.

sections.heading: 5. Colostrum Is the First Milk
paragraphs: In the first days after birth, the breasts produce colostrum. It is often thick and yellowish and contains concentrated nutrients and protective components. A newborn's stomach is small, so early feeds may involve only a small amount.

The World Health Organization recommends supporting breastfeeding as soon as possible after birth, ideally within the first hour when mother and baby are ready and medically stable. Families should receive practical help if feeding is difficult.

sections.heading: 6. A Mother's Body Needs Time to Recover
paragraphs: After delivery, the uterus gradually contracts and becomes smaller. Vaginal bleeding, tiredness, abdominal afterpains, breast changes, and soreness can occur during recovery. The details depend partly on whether the baby was born vaginally or by caesarean section.

Postnatal care includes checking the mother's vital signs, bleeding, uterine recovery, wounds where relevant, and emotional well-being. Heavy bleeding, fever, or feeling seriously unwell should be assessed urgently by a health professional.

sections.heading: 7. Newborns Must Adapt to Life Outside the Womb
paragraphs: Before birth, the baby receives oxygen and nutrients through the placenta. After birth, the newborn begins breathing with the lungs and adjusting to changes in temperature, feeding, and the surrounding environment.

Health professionals check the baby's breathing, temperature, colour, activity, and general condition. Some babies lose a little weight during the first few days; feeding and weight should be monitored to make sure the baby is progressing well.

sections.heading: 8. Becoming a First-Time Mother Is Also an Emotional Transition
paragraphs: The arrival of a first baby can bring happiness, relief, worry, exhaustion, and uncertainty—sometimes all at once. Learning a newborn's feeding cues, sleep patterns, and ways of communicating takes time.

Support from a partner, family, and healthcare professionals can make the early days easier. If sadness or anxiety is intense, lasts, or makes it difficult to care for oneself or the baby, the mother should be encouraged to seek professional help.

articles.closing: A baby's first cry is often remembered as the beginning of a new chapter. But childbirth is also a physical event for the mother, followed by recovery and adjustment. The newborn needs care and protection, and the mother needs care, rest, and support too. Every birth is different, but both deserve attention throughout the first days of life.

articles.title: 10 Amazing Facts About the Human Body That Will Surprise You
articles.description: Discover 10 fascinating facts about the human body, from your constantly beating heart to the remarkable abilities of your bones, skin, blood, and senses.
articles.dek: Your body performs extraordinary tasks every second. Explore ten fascinating facts about the systems that keep you alive.
articles.intro: The human body is one of nature's most fascinating and complex systems. Every second, countless biological processes take place inside us, even when we are sleeping, relaxing, or simply sitting still. From the heart that pumps blood to the bones that support our structure, the body performs remarkable tasks that most people rarely stop to consider. Here are ten science-based facts that may change the way you look at yourself.

sections.heading: 1. Your Heart Beats Around 100,000 Times a Day
paragraphs: An adult heart typically beats tens of thousands of times each day. A commonly used estimate is about 100,000 beats in 24 hours, although the actual number varies with age, activity, health, and resting heart rate.
Your heart keeps pumping blood to deliver oxygen and nutrients throughout your body. It continues working while you sleep, without requiring conscious control.

sections.heading: 2. Babies Have More Bones Than Adults
paragraphs: A newborn has around 270 to 300 bones or bone elements, depending on how they are counted. Most adults have 206 bones.
As a child grows, some bones gradually fuse together. This is one reason the adult skeleton has fewer separate bones than a newborn's skeleton.

sections.heading: 3. Your Skin Is Your Largest Organ
paragraphs: The skin is the body's largest organ by surface area and mass. It forms a protective barrier, helps regulate temperature, reduces water loss, and contains sensory receptors.
Those receptors help you detect touch, pressure, and temperature, allowing you to respond to your surroundings.

sections.heading: 4. Red Blood Cells Usually Live for About 120 Days
paragraphs: Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to tissues throughout the body. They contain haemoglobin, a protein that binds oxygen.
A typical red blood cell circulates for about 120 days before it is removed, mainly by the spleen and liver. The body continually makes new blood cells to replace aging ones.

sections.heading: 5. Your Bones Are Living Tissue
paragraphs: Bones are not lifeless structures. They contain living cells, blood vessels, and nerves, and they are continually renewed through a process called bone remodeling.
Bones support the body, protect organs, store minerals, and contain marrow that produces blood cells.

sections.heading: 6. Your Heart Begins Beating Before Birth
paragraphs: The developing heart starts to beat very early in pregnancy, around the fifth to sixth week of gestational age when counted from the last menstrual period. This is well before birth.
The heart then develops and changes as the embryo and fetus grow, preparing to support circulation after delivery.

sections.heading: 7. Sweating Helps Cool Your Body
paragraphs: When your body becomes too warm, sweat glands release moisture onto the skin. As that sweat evaporates, it removes heat and helps cool you down.
Your brain and nervous system coordinate several temperature-control responses, including sweating, changes in skin blood flow, and shivering when you are cold.

sections.heading: 8. Bone Marrow Makes Important Blood Cells
paragraphs: Red bone marrow is a soft tissue inside certain bones. It produces red blood cells, many white blood cells, and platelets through a process called blood cell formation.
These cells have different jobs: red blood cells transport oxygen, white blood cells help defend against infection, and platelets help blood clot.

sections.heading: 9. Sunlight Helps Your Skin Make Vitamin D
paragraphs: When skin is exposed to ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation, it begins a process that allows the body to produce vitamin D. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium and supports bone health.

The amount produced varies with factors such as skin pigmentation, age, location, season, clothing, and time outdoors. Too much UV exposure can damage skin, so sensible sun protection remains important.

sections.heading: 10. The Smallest Bone Is Inside Your Ear
paragraphs: The stapes, one of the three tiny bones in the middle ear, is the smallest bone in the human body. It is only a few millimetres long.
Together, the middle-ear bones transmit vibrations from the eardrum toward the inner ear, helping make hearing possible.

Your skin does much more than you might imagine!

Once they become old, they are removed from circulation and replaced by newly produced red blood cells. Your body is constantly renewing itself!

images.caption: Did you know that your bones contain a remarkable blood cell factory? Inside certain bones, a soft tissue called bone marrow produces essential blood cells every day. Red blood cells carry oxygen, white blood cells help fight infections, and platelets help stop bleeding when you get injured. Without healthy bone marrow, your body would struggle to maintain its blood supply and immune defenses. The human body is truly incredible!

However, excessive sun exposure can damage your skin, so protecting yourself from harmful UV radiation is important too!

bibleVerse.text: “I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made.”

articles.closing: The human body is an extraordinary biological system. From a heart that beats while you sleep to bones that continually renew themselves, your body performs countless remarkable processes every day. The more we learn about anatomy and physiology, the more we can appreciate the systems that make everyday life possible. Which of these ten facts surprised you the most? Share your thoughts and discover more with Jaziel Story.
